paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ξενοφῶν περὶ τῆς Σωκράτους ἀπολογίας γράφει. οὐκ ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ παρῆν, ἀλλὰ τὸν Ἑρμογένην μάρτυρα τοῦ λόγου παρέχει. ζητεῖ δὲ διὰ τί ὁ Σωκράτης μεγαληγόρως εἶπεν. καὶ ἄλλοι περὶ αὐτοῦ γεγράφασιν· ὁ Ξενοφῶν δὲ οἴεται δεῖν τὴν γνώμην τοῦ ἀνδρὸς δηλοῦν, ἵνα μὴ ἡ μεγαληγορία ἀφροσύνη δοκῇ εἶναι. ἡ οὖν διήγησις ἔχει σκοπόν.

Ὁ Ἑρμογένης ὁρῶν τὸν Σωκράτη περὶ ἄλλων διαλεγόμενον ἐθαύμαζεν. ἡ δίκη παρεσκευάζετο, οἱ δὲ κατήγοροι οὐκ ἡσύχαζον. τὰ μὲν ὀνόματα τῶν κατηγόρων ἐν τῇ πόλει ἠκούετο, ὁ δὲ φίλος περὶ τῆς σωτηρίας ἐφρόντιζεν. ἠρώτα οὖν εἰ δεῖ τὸν Σωκράτη καὶ τὴν ἀπολογίαν σκοπεῖν. οὐ γὰρ ἀρκέσειν ἐνόμιζεν τὸ δίκαιον, ἐὰν οἱ δικασταὶ μὴ πεισθῶσιν.

Ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης ἀπεκρίνατο ὅτι ὁ βίος αὐτῷ πρὸς τὴν ἀπολογίαν παρεσκεύασται. οὐ γὰρ ἀδικῶν διέζη, ἀλλὰ τὰ δίκαια πράττων. τὰ δὲ ἔργα, ἃ οἱ φίλοι τεθέανται, οὐκ ὀλίγην μαρτυρίαν παρέχει. ἡ ἀπολογία οὐ λόγος ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ κεκοσμημένος μόνον ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βίος πολὺν χρόνον ἐξεταζόμενος. οὕτω τὴν προπαρασκευὴν ἑρμηνεύει.

Ὁ Ἑρμογένης οὐκ εὐθὺς πέπεισται. ἐν γὰρ τοῖς δικαστηρίοις οἱ μὲν ἄδικοι ἀποφεύγουσιν, οἱ δὲ δίκαιοι κατακρίνονται. δεῖ οὖν καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀκουόντων γνώμην λέγειν. ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης περὶ τοῦ δαιμονίου διηγεῖται. ὅτε πρὸς τὴν ἀπολογίαν ἐτράπετο, ἐναντίον αὐτῷ ἐγένετο τὸ σημεῖον. ταύτην τὴν ἀπόκρισιν ὁ Ἑρμογένης μετέδωκε τῷ Ξενοφῶντι.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης καὶ τὸ γῆρας σκοπεῖ. φοβεῖται μὴ ὁ χρόνος τὴν μνήμην καὶ τὴν διάνοιαν βλάπτῃ. ὁ παρὼν βίος αὐτῷ ἱκανὸς δοκεῖ, καὶ τὸν θάνατον οὐ πάντων τῶν κακῶν μέγιστον νομίζει. οὐ τοῦτο διδάσκει ὁ Ξενοφῶν, ὅτι πᾶς ἄνθρωπος τὴν αὐτὴν κρίσιν ποιεῖται· τὴν τοῦ Σωκράτους γνώμην ἐξηγεῖται, καθ᾽ ἣν ἐκεῖνος τῇ δίκῃ προσέρχεται.

Ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ ἀσκήσει διακρίνομεν τὸ γενόμενον καὶ τὸ νῦν ὑπάρχον. ὁ λόγος ἐγράφη· νῦν γέγραπται. ὁ φίλος ἐπείσθη· νῦν πέπεισται. πρὶν τὸν ἄλλον ἐλθεῖν, ἤδη ἐπέπειστο. τὰ μὲν πρῶτα ῥήματα πράξεις ὡς ὅλας δηλοῖ, τὰ δὲ ἄλλα τὴν ἐκ τῶν πράξεων κατάστασιν. μὴ πάντα τῷ αὐτῷ τρόπῳ μεταφράζωμεν.

Τέλος ἐρωτῶμεν ποία ἀπολογία τῷ δικαστῇ πιστοτέρα φαίνεται. ὁ κεκοσμημένος λόγος δύναται ὠφελεῖν, ἀλλὰ δεῖ καὶ τὰ ἔργα ἐξετάζειν. ὁ δὲ ἐπαινούμενος βίος οὐκ ἀπαλλάττει τὸν ἀκροατὴν τοῦ κρίνειν. τὸν μὲν φίλον ἀκούομεν, τὸν δὲ συγγραφέα ἐξετάζομεν, καὶ τὸν λόγον πρὸς τὰ τεκμήρια συγκρίνομεν. οὕτως ἡ φιλία καὶ ἡ κρίσις ἅμα μένουσιν.

reading.translation:
Xenophon writes about Socrates’ defense. He was not present in the court, but offers Hermogenes as a witness to the account. He asks why Socrates spoke so loftily. Others too have written about him; Xenophon thinks that the man’s intention must be made clear, so that the lofty speech may not appear foolishness. The narrative therefore has a purpose.

Hermogenes was surprised to see Socrates discussing other matters. The trial was being prepared, and the accusers were not idle. The accusers’ names were being heard in the city, while the friend worried about Socrates’ safety. He therefore asked whether Socrates ought also to consider his defense. He thought that justice would not suffice if the jurors were not persuaded.

Socrates replied that his life had been prepared by him as a defense. For he had lived not by doing wrong but by acting justly. The deeds that his friends have observed provide substantial testimony. A defense is not merely a speech adorned in a single day, but also a life examined over a long time. In this way he interprets preparation.

Hermogenes is not immediately convinced. In the courts the unjust are sometimes acquitted and the just condemned. One must therefore speak with the listeners’ judgment in mind. Socrates, however, tells of the divine sign. When he turned to preparing his defense, the sign opposed him. Hermogenes communicated this response to Xenophon.

Socrates also considers old age. He fears that time may damage memory and understanding. His present life seems sufficient to him, and he does not regard death as the greatest of all evils. Xenophon does not teach here that every person makes the same judgment; he explains Socrates’ view, in accordance with which Socrates approaches the trial.

In our exercise we distinguish what happened from what now holds. The speech was written; now it stands written. The friend was persuaded; now he is convinced. Before the other person arrived, he had already been persuaded. The first verbs present actions as wholes, while the others present the state arising from the actions. Let us not translate everything in the same way.

Finally we ask what kind of defense appears more credible to a judge. An adorned speech can help, but the deeds must also be examined. A praised life does not release the listener from judging. We listen to the friend, examine the writer, and compare the account with the evidence. In this way friendship and judgment remain together.

sections.title: 1. Perfect middle/passive: formation and state
body: The perfect commonly presents a resulting state: λέλυται can mean “has been released” and hence “is free.” The aorist ἐλύθη narrates the release as a whole. The perfect is not simply a more distant past tense. In the middle/passive, endings attach directly to the perfect stem, without a thematic vowel.

Learn λέλυμαι, λέλυσαι, λέλυται, λελύμεθα, λέλυσθε, λέλυνται. Identify the reduplicated stem λελυ- and the ending. Middle versus passive interpretation depends on the verb and context: πέπεισμαι, “I am convinced,” describes the subject’s state. Contract verbs often lengthen their stem vowel before perfect endings, as τετίμημαι.

sections.title: 2. Reduplication, vowels, and consonant stems
body: A simple consonant often reduplicates with ε: λύω → λέλυμαι. Aspirated consonants use the corresponding unaspirated sound in reduplication: θύω → τέθυμαι, not an initial θ twice. Initial vowels commonly lengthen: ἀδικέω → ἠδίκημαι. Clusters and irregular verbs require principal parts; do not generate every perfect by repeating the first written letter.

Consonant stems change at the junction with endings: γράφω gives γέγραμμαι, γέγραψαι, γέγραπται; πράττω gives πέπραγμαι, πέπραξαι, πέπρακται. Dental stems often yield σ before the ending, as πεπείσμαι. Consonant-stem third plurals frequently use a participle with εἰσί: γεγραμμένοι εἰσί.

sections.title: 3. Perfect participles and infinitives
body: The perfect middle/passive participle uses -μένος, -μένη, -μένον, normally accented on the syllable before the ending: λελυμένος. It agrees in gender, number, and case with its noun. ὁ λελυμένος, with an article, can mean “the released man”; without an article it can supply a circumstance or predicate.

The perfect middle/passive infinitive is λελύσθαι. In indirect statement it reports a state resulting from prior action; after other governing verbs interpret aspect and construction. A participle plus εἰμί can form a periphrastic perfect, and with ἦν a past state. Keep agreement visible rather than treating the whole expression as indeclinable.

sections.title: 4. Pluperfect middle/passive
body: The pluperfect places the resulting state at a past reference point: ἐλέλυτο, “he had been released.” It normally adds an augment before the reduplicated stem and secondary middle/passive endings. Learn ἐλελύμην, ἐλέλυσο, ἐλέλυτο, ἐλελύμεθα, ἐλέλυσθε, ἐλέλυντο.

Compare ἐπείσθη, “he was persuaded,” πέπεισται, “he is convinced,” and ἐπέπειστο, “he had been persuaded.” The pluperfect’s past viewpoint can be established by another event, such as the friend’s arrival. Consonant stems may use a periphrastic form, as γεγραμμένοι ἦσαν; agreement still matters.

sections.title: 5. Dative of agent and other datives
body: With perfect passive forms, a dative can mark the agent: ταῦτα ἡμῖν πέπρακται, “These things have been done by us.” It is particularly natural with a resulting state viewed as someone’s completed work. Ordinary passive agents can also be expressed with ὑπό plus genitive; a dative is not the universal agent construction in every tense.

Compare the agent with possession, recipient, and means. In δῶρον τῷ φίλῳ δίδοται, “a gift is given to the friend,” the friend is recipient. In λόγῳ πείθει, “he persuades by speech,” the dative expresses means. Ask who performs the action, who receives it, and what instrument or relation the phrase supplies.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Apology
body: Xenophon’s Apology of Socrates is a short defense of the philosopher’s conduct at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE. “Apology” here means a defense, not an expression of regret. The work opens by asking why Socrates spoke with such elevated self-confidence. Xenophon wants the reader to understand the intention behind that manner, including Socrates’ judgment about his age, life, and approaching death. The choice of opening question shapes everything that follows.

The work moves from a conversation with Hermogenes before the trial to selected courtroom exchanges, reactions, the verdict, and Socrates’ response. It does not attempt to reproduce every procedural stage or every word spoken. Xenophon explicitly names Hermogenes as an informant in section 2. That is valuable evidence about a chain of testimony, but it does not turn the finished literary work into a transcript. Ask when the narrator summarizes, when Socrates answers an objection, and when a friend’s report supplies the connection.

Plato wrote a different Apology, and the two works should be read as distinct presentations. Do not silently import Plato’s famous phrases or penalty proposals into Xenophon’s account. Xenophon also defends Socrates across the four books of the Memorabilia, where conversations and habits provide a broader portrait. Read sections 1–9 for the preparation, 10–26 for the selected trial account, and the closing sections for the remembered aftermath. The complete translation linked here makes it possible to see the lesson’s excerpt in its argumentative setting. Across Lessons 45–47, notice how preparation, reputation, and courtroom reporting each illuminate a different part of Xenophon’s purpose.

sections.title: A defense made from a life
body: Hermogenes is concerned that Socrates has not prepared the kind of defense that may persuade a jury. Socrates answers by treating his conduct as preparation. The disagreement is about what counts as an adequate defense: a persuasive presentation on the day, a record of behavior, or both.

Xenophon’s account also connects Socrates’ attitude with his age and his judgment about death. This explains the author’s portrait of a particular person. It is not a general lesson that defendants should refuse practical preparation or that every persuasive appeal is dishonest.

sections.title: Hermogenes as informant
body: Apology 2 explicitly names Hermogenes as a source. Xenophon was not an eyewitness in the courtroom. His reliance on a named associate gives us an identifiable link in the testimony, but the finished work still selects, arranges, and interprets material.

Compare three layers: Socrates’ reported words, Hermogenes’ report, and Xenophon’s authorial purpose. A sentence can be valuable evidence while still needing these distinctions. Do not invent a date or setting for the transmission of the report when the text does not provide one.

sections.title: Speech, conduct, and persuasion
body: Prepare two short defenses of a fictional decision: one based on a person’s record of conduct, another on the immediate circumstances. Identify what evidence each needs. Neither exercise should teach that emotion is always deceitful or that a good reputation makes examination unnecessary.

Translate the perfect-system examples as a separate teaching passage, then return to the reported conversation. Your complete translation should distinguish a completed act from a state that now holds and from a state that already held at an earlier point.
